questions.question: Who among the following formed the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha in 1929?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Swami Sahajanand Saraswati**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Swami Sahajanand Saraswati was a prominent peasant leader in India and was deeply involved in the peasant movement.
 
• He founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (BPKS) in 1929 to address the issues of peasants and farmers in Bihar.
 
• The BPKS played a crucial role in mobilizing peasants against the zamindari system and for the rights of tenant farmers.
 
• Swami Sahajanand Saraswati later became the president of the All India Kisan Sabha, a nationwide peasant organization, further amplifying his influence in the peasant movement in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Peasant Movement in India:**

 
 
• The peasant movement in India was a series of political movements for the rights of the agricultural workers and against the feudal land system.
 
• These movements were significant in shaping the agrarian policies of the country and addressing issues like land reforms, tenancy rights, and fair wages.
 
 
 
• **Zamindari System:**
 
 
• The Zamindari system was a traditional land revenue system in India where landlords or zamindars collected rent from the peasants and paid a portion to the British colonial government.
 
• This system led to the exploitation of peasants, high rents, and forced labor, causing widespread agrarian distress.
 
 
 
• **All India Kisan Sabha (AIKS):**
 
 
• The AIKS was formed in 1936 as a national organization to address the issues faced by peasants across India.
 
• It worked towards the abolition of the zamindari system, fair land distribution, and better living conditions for agricultural workers.
 
 
 
• **Swami Sahajanand Saraswati's Contributions:**
 
 
• He was a key figure in the peasant movement and worked tirelessly for the upliftment of the agrarian community.
 
• His efforts led to significant reforms in the agrarian sector, and he is remembered as a champion of peasant rights in India.

questions.question: What were the main obstacles during the industrial development of India at the time of independence?

• The capital formation was very low, and there was a lack of institutions to provide long-term finance for industrial projects.
 
• Industrial infrastructure was underdeveloped, and there was an absence of modern technology, which required significant investment to upgrade.
 
• The government's focus was on agricultural development and poverty alleviation, which led to limited allocation of funds for industrialization.

• India had a large pool of labor, but the majority were unskilled and engaged in agriculture.
 
• There was a need for training and skill development to make the workforce suitable for industrial employment.
 
 
 
• **Land for industrial establishment:**
 
 
• Availability of land was not a major issue, but the acquisition process was cumbersome and often faced resistance from local communities.

• They attacked the policemen who intervened.
 
• The planters, in response to this, increased the rents and evicted the farmers which led to more agitations.
 
 
 
• In April 1860, all the farmers in the Barasat division of the districts Nadia and Pabna went on a strike and refused to grow indigo.
 
• The strike spread to other parts of Bengal.
 
• The anger of the peasants exploded in 1859 when led by Digambar Biswas and Bishnu Biswas of Nadia district, they decided not to grow indigo under duress and resisted the physical pressure of the planters.
 
• The revolt was suppressed and many farmers were slaughtered by the government and some of the zamindars.
 
• The revolt was backed by the Bengali intelligentsia, Muslims, and missionaries. The whole of the rural population supported the revolt.
 
• The press also supported the revolt and played its part in portraying the plight of the farmers and fighting for their cause.

From the above, we can conclude that the 'Indigo Revolt' took place in Bengal in March 1859.

• The **Regulating Act of 1773** was the first attempt by the British government to regulate the affairs of the East India Company in India.
 
• It established a system of dual control, with both the company and the British government involved in administration.
 
• This act marked the beginning of British parliamentary control over India.
 
 
 
• **Rowlatt Act**__
 __
 
• The **Rowlatt Act**, also known as the **Black Act**, was passed in 1919 by the British Government in India.
 
• It allowed the government to imprison any person suspected of terrorism without trial for up to two years.
 
• This act led to widespread anger and protests, including the infamous Jallianwala Bagh massacre.
 
 
 
• **Simon Commission**__
 
 
• The **Simon Commission** was a group of seven British Members of Parliament that was sent to India in 1927 to study constitutional reform.
 
• It was met with strong opposition from Indian leaders because it did not include any Indian members.
 
• The slogan "**Simon Go Back**" was popular during the protests against the commission.
